name: Minoxidil
lead: Minoxidil is a vasodilator that doubles as one of the two most widely used drugs for pattern hair loss. Applied to the scalp as a liquid or foam, it is used to thicken thinning hair and, in some users, to regrow hair at the crown, and it is sold over the counter as Rogaine and as many generics.[1][2] The same molecule, taken by mouth at much higher doses, treats severe high blood pressure under the brand Loniten.[1] More recently, low-dose oral minoxidil has become a widely prescribed off-label option for hair loss, and minoxidil is also used by people who want fuller beards and eyebrows.[1][37]

For appearance, minoxidil works on follicles that are shrinking but still present. In trials and clinical reviews it increases hair counts and shaft thickness, with benefits appearing over about two to four months and a maximum at around twelve months; results are maintained only while treatment continues, and hair density returns toward placebo levels roughly 24 weeks after stopping.[1] Because it acts independently of androgens, it is commonly combined with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor such as finasteride, which works on the hormonal side of male pattern hair loss.[7][8]

Research on minoxidil spans four decades, from 1980s clinical trials through multiple meta-analyses to 2024 randomised comparisons of oral and topical forms.[26][4][6] Its side effects are mostly scalp irritation and unwanted hair on the face with topical use, and fluid retention, fast heartbeat, dizziness and hypertrichosis with oral use, with rare serious cardiac effects described mainly at hypertension doses.[1][7]

chain: Applied to the scalp (or taken orally under medical care)
Opens potassium channels in follicles and prolongs the growth phase
Miniaturised follicles thicken and more hairs are in growth
Denser, fuller-looking hair while use continues
angle.text: Minoxidil is used to thicken thinning hair and regrow hair along the crown and, off-label, to fill in beards and eyebrows. People typically apply it twice daily to the scalp or beard, or use a prescribed low-dose tablet, and look for changes over several months, with continued use needed to keep the result.

paras: Topical minoxidil in 5 percent foam, 5 percent solution and 2 percent solution is FDA-approved for androgenetic alopecia in men and women.[2] Wikipedia states that its effectiveness has largely been demonstrated in younger men with hair loss of under five years, that it is less effective when the area of loss is large, and that the over-the-counter label indicates vertex (crown) hair loss only.[1] It increases hair counts and thickens individual hairs, with benefit usually visible after two to four months and peaking near twelve months.[1] The US label for a 5 percent product states it is for men only, is not intended for frontal baldness or a receding hairline, and warns that it is flammable.[10]

Users apply liquids or foams to the scalp, typically twice a day, and many pair minoxidil with finasteride or dutasteride, microneedling or other measures for hair loss; the drug itself does not act on androgens.[1][7][8] Wikipedia notes that almost all topical users stop within a year, and attributes this to cost, skin reactions and the daily routine.[1]

Minoxidil has also been studied for beard growth, including in transgender men, and is used off-label on beards and eyebrows; Wikipedia further lists at least six clinical studies in nail disorders.[1] Foam, liquid and spray forms exist, and liquids contain propylene glycol to aid absorption, which can irritate some scalps.[1]

Oral minoxidil at hypertension doses is reserved for severe high blood pressure not controlled by at least two other agents plus a diuretic.[1] Low-dose oral minoxidil is used off-label for hair loss and is considered an alternative for those who have difficulty with topical formulations.[1] Dermatology Times quotes dermatologists who say it is widely prescribed worldwide, is off-label and is often used for patients who will not use topicals; one noted that topical products can leave hair feeling greasy.[37] Sublingual minoxidil is under study, with a phase 3 trial in men (NCT06924632) listed as completed.[1][11] Registered trials have also tested it for endocrine therapy-induced alopecia in breast cancer and oral minoxidil in recurrent ovarian cancer.[12][13]

A 48-week randomised, double-blind trial in men compared 5 percent topical minoxidil, 2 percent minoxidil and placebo.[14] A comprehensive review states that in a five-year study 2 percent minoxidil reached peak growth in men at year one and declined after, and that 5 percent solution and foam did not differ significantly from 2 percent in efficacy.[2] The same review reported that after six months oral 5 mg per day was significantly more effective than topical 5 percent and 2 percent in male androgenetic alopecia, and that 0.5 to 5 mg per day may be effective for female pattern hair loss.[2]

The 2017 meta-analysis found 5 percent and 2 percent minoxidil in men and 2 percent in women superior to placebo, alongside 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser light.[4] A 2022 comparison ranked probable efficacy as dutasteride 0.5 mg, finasteride 5 mg, oral minoxidil 5 mg, finasteride 1 mg, then oral minoxidil 0.25 mg.[7] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies concluded that over-the-counter, prescription and procedural treatments, topical minoxidil among them, promote hair growth, and favoured an individualised, multifaceted approach.[15]

Wikipedia reports that minoxidil does not appear to prevent hair loss in the long term and that the benefit is fully reversible, with the label advising it be used indefinitely to maintain results.[1] Dermatology Times quotes one clinician saying many clinical studies report response rates above 65 percent for low-dose oral use, while noting response varies between patients.[37]

Human trials are extensive. Randomised trials include the 5 percent versus 2 percent versus placebo trial in men, a 2024 randomised trial of low-dose oral versus topical minoxidil, the 2024 JAMA Dermatology trial of oral versus topical minoxidil in men, a trial of 0.25 percent finasteride with 3 percent minoxidil versus minoxidil alone, and a trial comparing pumpkin seed oil with 5 percent minoxidil foam in female pattern hair loss.[14][16][6][17][18]

Registered studies include a phase 3 trial of 5 percent foam in 352 men with male pattern hair loss (NCT00151515), phase 3 trials in women (NCT01145625, n=322; NCT00958750, n=113), a microarray analysis of scalp biopsies after treatment (NCT01309191), and a topical finasteride-minoxidil combination study (NCT05990400).[19][20][21][22][23] A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology offers recommendations for safe and effective topical and oral use, and a 2025 article in PubMed Central reviews oral minoxidil in alopecia.[24][25]

An early 1987 review described minoxidil's use in male pattern alopecia and alopecia areata, and found side effects almost entirely cutaneous in patients without cardiovascular disease.[26] A 2019 review describes it as the mainstay treatment for androgenetic alopecia and an off-label option for other hair loss conditions.[29] Wikipedia also reports that after the FDA's 1988 approval, the agency said 39 percent of men studied had moderate to dense growth at the crown.[1]

Topical minoxidil is generally well tolerated; common effects are itching, local irritation and unwanted hair growth elsewhere, and alcohol and propylene glycol in some products may dry the scalp and cause dandruff or contact dermatitis.[1] Temporary shedding is described for both topical and oral forms.[1] The US label for a 5 percent product advises against use by women, people under 18, and those with a red, inflamed or irritated scalp.[10] About 1.2 to 1.4 percent of a topical dose is absorbed, and serum levels are usually very low.[1][2]

Side effects of oral minoxidil include salt and water retention with edema, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches and hypertrichosis.[1] Hypertrichosis is dose-dependent and, according to dermatologists quoted by Dermatology Times, tends to show on the upper lip, sideburns, forehead and forearms; some clinicians add other medicines to limit it.[37] Pericarditis, pericardial and pleural effusion and cardiac tamponade have been implicated, with pericardial effusion in about 3 percent at hypertension doses; Wikipedia says these are much less common at the low doses used for hair loss.[1] The oral drug carries a boxed warning for pericardial effusion, according to Dermatology Times.[37] Absolute contraindications include pheochromocytoma, prior pericardial effusion or tamponade, and pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1] Low-dose oral minoxidil's effect on blood pressure is discussed on tressless.com.[27]

Wikipedia reports that aspirin may reduce topical minoxidil's effect by inhibiting the sulfotransferase that activates it, and that paracetamol and salicylic acid may similarly interfere.[1] It describes a seven-year-old who ingested a teaspoon of a minoxidil product and had hypotension and tachycardia for about 40 hours, and says the drug is highly toxic to dogs and cats even in tiny amounts.[1]

The mechanism of hair growth is not fully understood.[1][28] Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by sulfotransferase (SULT1A1 in follicles) into minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels; reviews also describe vasodilator, anti-inflammatory, Wnt/beta-catenin-inducing and antiandrogen actions, and effects on the length of anagen and telogen phases.[1][2] Expression of SULT1A1 has been reported to predict response to topical minoxidil, so people with higher follicular sulfotransferase activity may respond better.[1][2] Growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and IGF-1 are induced in dermal papilla cells, and the effect is described as involving adenosine signalling.[1] The early shedding some users see is explained as resting follicles being pushed out and replaced by thicker hairs.[1]

Oral absorption is about 90 percent or more with peak levels in 30 to 60 minutes; the plasma half-life is about 4 hours, although the blood-pressure effect lasts much longer.[1][7] Only about 1.2 to 1.4 percent of topical minoxidil is absorbed through the scalp, with serum levels usually below 5 ng/mL.[1][2]

Upjohn, later part of Pfizer, was exploring an ulcer treatment in the 1950s; the compound failed in dogs for ulcers but proved a powerful vasodilator, and the company synthesised minoxidil in 1963.[1] It was introduced for high blood pressure in 1971, and the FDA approved oral tablets as Loniten in 1979.[1] Physicians noticed hypertrichosis in patients, and University of Colorado dermatologist Charles Chidsey ran studies that showed unexpected hair growth; former University of Miami resident Guinter Kahn and Paul Grant had also experimented with a topical solution, leading to a roughly decade-long patent dispute that ended with a combined patent in 1986 and royalties to Kahn and Grant.[1] Doctors prescribed Loniten off-label to balding patients through the 1980s.[1]

The FDA approved minoxidil for hair loss in men in August 1988 as Rogaine; the agency rejected the name Regain as misleading.[1] A version for women followed in 1991, and in February 1996 the FDA approved over-the-counter sale and generics.[1] A 5 percent formulation was approved for nonprescription sale in 1998, a 5 percent foam in 2006, and generic foams in 2017.[1] Men's Rogaine went off-patent in January 2006 and women's Rogaine in February 2014.[1] A 2017 study noted that foam products marketed to women cost about 40 percent more than those for men.[1]

Low-dose oral minoxidil emerged around 2015 through work by Australian dermatologist Rodney Sinclair and colleagues.[1][37] After an August 2022 New York Times article headlined that an old medicine grows new hair for pennies a day, interest in the drug rose sharply.[1] Extended-release and sublingual formulations were in phase 3 trials as of September 2025.[1]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities
paras: Minoxidil is the default growth treatment in hair-loss communities, usually listed next to finasteride, dutasteride and microneedling. Forums such as community.tressless.com and hairlosstalk.com host threads on oral minoxidil, including users announcing they are starting it, discussion of oral dosage and sources, and a thread on low-dose oral minoxidil and blood pressure.[30][31][27] Beard and eyebrow use is widely discussed in appearance communities.[9][1]

On T Nation, men discuss the Kirkland store brand, add low-dose oral minoxidil alongside testosterone, or ask whether Rogaine would affect natural status in competition; a user also says the drug has about 40 percent good responders on topical use.[32][33][34][35]

Brands include Rogaine and Regaine for topical use and Loniten for tablets, with many store brands and generics worldwide, plus combination products with other actives.[1] Topical minoxidil is sold over the counter in many countries; oral minoxidil requires a prescription, and its use for hair loss is off-label.[1][2]

lore.intro: Minoxidil is discussed as the baseline growth treatment in hair-loss communities, with growing interest in low-dose oral use as an alternative to topical application.[30][31][36]

claims.claim: Minoxidil regrows and thickens hair independent of hormones
claims.believers: Users report using it alone or with finasteride and describe family members with good results.[34][8]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses show topical minoxidil beats placebo, though the effect depends on continued use.[4][1]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil works better than topical and is easier to stick with
claims.believers: Forum posters announce switching to oral minoxidil and trade views on dosing sources.[30][31]
claims.experts: A 2024 JAMA Dermatology trial and other randomised trials compared oral and topical forms; a review reports oral 5 mg more effective than topical at six months, but oral minoxidil is off-label and has cardiovascular effects.[6][16][2]

claims.claim: Low-dose oral minoxidil does not affect blood pressure
claims.believers: A tressless.com thread argues low-dose oral minoxidil does not significantly affect blood pressure.[27]
claims.experts: Reviews list hypotension, tachycardia and edema as dose-dependent oral effects, and Wikipedia says cardiovascular complications are rarer at low doses.[7][1]

claims.claim: Early shedding means it is working
claims.believers: Users describe an initial shedding phase before regrowth, consistent with community advice to be patient.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists temporary shedding as a known effect and explains minoxidil may push telogen follicles to shed before replacement by thicker hairs.[1]

claims.believers: Beard-growth use is widely discussed in appearance communities.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states minoxidil has been studied for beard growth, including in transgender men.[1]

claims.claim: Using minoxidil would disqualify someone as a natural lifter
claims.believers: One forum comment jokingly asks whether Rogaine would cost natural status.[35]
claims.experts: Minoxidil is not described as an anabolic agent; it is a vasodilator used for hair loss.[1]

claims.claim: Topical minoxidil is messy and unpleasant so people quit
claims.believers: Posters describe greasy hair and a twice-daily routine as reasons for switching to oral use.[30][31]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that almost all topical users stop within a year, and dermatologists quoted in Dermatology Times cite greasiness, cost and skin reactions as adherence problems.[1][37]

claims.claim: Hair gained on minoxidil is lost again if you stop
claims.believers: Community members describe staying on it indefinitely to hold density.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the effect is fully reversible and density falls to placebo levels within about 24 weeks of stopping.[1]
